recommended_change.label: buf64M-irqpin-coal500-threadpin
host_commands: i=0; for irq in $(grep enp4s0f0np0- /proc/interrupts | grep -v xdp | awk -F: '{print $1}'); do echo $((2*i)) > /proc/irq/$irq/smp_affinity_list; i=$((i+1)); done
ethtool -C enp4s0f0np0 adaptive-rx off rx-usecs 500 tx-usecs 500

cat > /tmp/pin.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
old=$(pgrep -x named)
for i in $(seq 1 300); do p=$(pgrep -x named); if [ -n "$p" ] && [ "$p" != "$old" ]; then break; fi; sleep 1; done
sleep 5
p=$(pgrep -x named)
for t in /proc/$p/task/*; do c=$(cat $t/comm); case $c in isc-loop-*) n=$((10#${c#isc-loop-}));; named) n=0;; *) continue;; esac; taskset -pc $n ${t##*/}; done > /tmp/pin.log 2>&1
sleep 60
ps -T -o tid,comm,psr,pcpu -p $p >> /tmp/pin.log
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/pin.sh; rm -f /tmp/pin.log; setsid nohup /tmp/pin.sh > /dev/null 2>&1 < /dev/null &

summary:
RECOMMENDATION: buf64M-irqpin-coal500-threadpin (1.07M QPS; the same design with 16M buffers gave 1.06M). Baseline was 420k, so this is about 2.5x.
Config:
- named: udp-receive-buffer 67108864;
- sysctl: net.core.rmem_max = rmem_default = 64M
- stop irqbalance; pin the 16 RX-queue IRQs of enp4s0f0np0 1:1 to node-0 CPUs 0,2,...,30
- ethtool -C enp4s0f0np0 adaptive-rx off rx-usecs 500 tx-usecs 500
- after named starts, pin each event-loop thread isc-loop-N to CPU N (main "named" threads to CPU 0) with taskset

Confidence: high that it is about 1.05-1.07M. Two separate runs (16M and 64M buffers) gave the same per-level shape: about 99.99% answered at 1.0M, 99.95% at 1.05M, about 98.5% at 1.08M, about 97.3% at 1.1M.

Optional extra: adding mitigations=off on the kernel command line (needs a reboot; tuning made persistent with systemd units) scored 1.10M, the best single result. That run passed 1.1M at 99.5% against 97.3% without it, so the gain looks like about 3-4%. But it is one sample, its repeat was lost to the testbed fault below, and it disables CPU-vulnerability protection on an Ivy Bridge server. I would only use it if that risk is acceptable.

WHAT LIMITS THIS SERVER (in the order found):
1. Socket receive buffers. At baseline, every lost query was a UDP RcvbufError; there were no NIC, softnet or backlog drops. Raising rmem and udp-receive-buffer to 16M: 420k to 620k.
2. Interrupt and wakeup overhead per packet. With adaptive coalescing (about 60us), named spent about 30us of logical-CPU time per query and woke up per packet (about 175k context switches/s at only 100k QPS).
   - rx-usecs 200: 830k
   - rx-usecs 500: 950k
   - rx-usecs 800: 920k, so flat; the sfc driver rejects values of 900 and above
   At 800k, named used 22 CPUs instead of 28 and context switches fell from about 175k/s to about 5k/s.
3. Uneven load across threads. Each named loop thread owns one reuseport socket that gets 1/32 of the flows. When the scheduler stacked two loop threads on one CPU, that socket overflowed even with 30% of the machine idle. Pinning each loop thread to its own CPU: 950k to 1.06-1.07M, with almost lossless answering below the knee.
4. Now plain CPU. Near 1.1M the 32 hyperthreads (16 Ivy Bridge cores) are saturated by named plus softirq. That is why mitigations=off now helps a little, though it showed nothing at 640k when the earlier limits applied.

Smaller findings:
- irqbalance had put up to 4 RX queues on one physical core. Pinning IRQs alone gave 640/730/700k against 620k, inside the noise, but it is the base for the later steps.
- No effect: C-state disable (620k), 64M buffers without the other fixes (680k), GRO off plus 4096 ring (910k).
- Harmful: reuseport no (440k; one shared socket collapses).

TESTBED ISSUE, PLEASE CHECK:
- Runs 8, 19 and 20 answered about 0.0015% (about 1 in 65,536) at every rate, down to 10k QPS. Each was the first measurement after a restore that rebooted the server.
- run 19 was an exact repeat of the config that had just scored 1.10M; run 20 repeated a no-reboot config that had scored 1.07M.
- In run 8 the server's UDP counters showed every query received and answered, and the NIC sent the replies; the clients still counted almost none.
- The 1/65,536 rate points to a corrupted 16-bit field, most likely the UDP checksum, after the reboot-restore. A non-reboot measurement cycle fixed it (run 9 worked after run 8).
- I count these as testbed artifacts, not config results, but the reboot-restore path or the boot-time profile script (apt upgrade, reinstalling bind and overwriting named.conf.options, running alongside the measurement) needs a look.

NEXT STEPS I'D TRY:
- Make the thread pinning permanent: a systemd unit, ideally with a fixed thread count.
- Repeat mitigations=off once more on a healthy testbed.
- Try one RX queue per physical core across both NUMA nodes.
- Try named -n 24 with IRQs kept on separate CPUs.
- Use perf to find where named's roughly 15-20us of core time per query goes.
